chunks: We also know that the appointment of the leader is obligatory after the Law, because in his appointment there is grace, for his bearing the performance of what no one else performs.

And with this, the empowerment is not realized by the people of resolution and contract from appointing one who is suitable for it specifically, according to the school of the people of justice, with whom our discourse is.
And with this, no one says: that the obligation of appointing the leader has fallen now, in that the empowerment from him has not occurred.
ai.seo_question: Why is the Imamate considered obligatory even if the Imam has not yet been publicly empowered?
ai.summary: This passage from Shaykh al-Tusi’s *Kitab al-Ghayba* clarifies the Shia doctrine of *Nass* (designation) and *Lutf* (divine grace), asserting that the Imamate remains an obligatory duty (*wajib*) regardless of whether the 'people of resolution' (*ahl al-hall wa-l-'aqd*) have successfully installed the Imam. It distinguishes between the ontological obligation of the Imamate and the practical condition of his political empowerment, ensuring that the absence of a visible ruler does not nullify the divine requirement for leadership.
